title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning & Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policy, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook structure. It is intended as the canonical guidance for service owners, on-call engineers, and product partners.

Scope and audience

- Applies to all production-facing services in the Redwood runtime, control plane, and customer-facing APIs.
- Audience: service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, product managers, and security/compliance stakeholders.

Principles

1) SLOs protect product velocity: set measurable targets that balance user experience and engineering throughput.
2) Error budgets are a shared contract between SRE and product; burns should drive action, not blame.
3) Capacity planning is proactive and data-driven; we plan for typical and peak distributions with explicit buffers.
4) Runbooks are executable, minimal, and regularly exercised.

Ownership and cadence

- Service owner: defines business requirements and acceptable risk.
- SRE owner: defines SLI instrumentation, alerting, and operational playbooks.
- Quarterly SLO review with product and SRE to adjust targets, based on metrics and business changes.

SLO framework

Key concepts

- SLI (Service Level Indicator): a measurable metric representing user-perceived reliability (e.g., request success rate, p99 latency).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): the target value for an SLI over a rolling period (commonly 30 days).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (the tolerated fraction of bad events).
- Burn rate: ratio of error budget consumption to expected consumption.

Canonical SLIs (examples)

- API success rate (2xx within expected request timeout) — primary availability SLI.
- Request latency p95 and p99 for the inference API (separate SLIs for small/long sequences).
- Embedding job completion success rate and median latency.
- KV cache hit rate for runtime caching layer.

Recommended SLO targets (example table)

Service | SLI | Window | Target
--- | --- | --- | ---
Public inference API (prod) | 99.95% success rate (30d) | 30d | 99.95%
Public inference API (p99 latency) | p99 latency < 2.5s (30d) | 30d | 99%
Embedding API | 99.9% success rate (30d) | 30d | 99.9%
Control plane (model rollouts) | 99.5% operation success (30d) | 30d | 99.5%
Dedicated customer endpoints | 99.99% success rate (30d) | 30d | 99.99%

Notes: Targets above are starting guidance. Individual services set concrete SLOs in collaboration with product. For premium/dedicated tiers, SLOs will be higher and contract-specific.

Error budget policy and response playbook

Definitions: error budget = (1 - SLO) * time window.

Burn rate thresholds (30-day window)

- Green: burn rate <= 1. Normal operations.
- Yellow: burn rate > 1 and <= 3 for a sustained 6-hour period -> Notify product, schedule focused reliability work in next sprint, increase monitoring cadence.
- Orange: burn rate > 3 for a sustained 3-hour period -> On-call lead to open a reliability incident; temporary mitigation prioritized; freeze non-critical releases for affected service.
- Red: burn rate > 10 for sustained 1 hour or SLO breach predicted -> Page SRE and product leadership; emergency remediation and rollback authority granted; incident review mandatory.

Automated enforcement and communication

- Burn rate alerts are surfaced in PagerDuty and Slack.
- Affected service channel must post: current burn rate, key metrics, mitigation plan, and follow-up owner.
- Product manager must be added to major-burn incidents.

Monitoring, alerting, and dashboards

Minimum monitoring for every service

- SLI dashboards (30d and 90d views).
- Error budget burn-rate dashboard.
- Top contributors to budget burn (region, model, route, request type).
- Synthetic transaction tests (runbook-critical flows every 1m to 5m).

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- SLI alert (warning): when 7-day rolling success rate is < SLO - 0.25% -> create ticket and notify SRE channel.
- Burn rate alert: when 30d burn rate crosses > 1.5 for 6 hours -> create an incident.
- Latency alerts: p95 > target for 15m, p99 for 5m -> page on-call for the service.

Operational tooling (approved stack)

- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term ingestion.
- Dashboards: Grafana with templated SLO panels.
- Tracing: Honeycomb / Jaeger for distributed traces.
- Logging: Loki / Elastic for application logs.
- Error aggregation: Sentry for backend exceptions.
- Incident management: PagerDuty for paging and runbook links, Slack for in-incident coordination.
- Ownership & runbook storage: Confluence (this space) with links to runbook JSONs.
- IaC for alerts/dashboards: Terraform + grafana-provider; alerts should be code-reviewed.

Capacity planning and forecasting

Goals

- Ensure SLOs are achievable under typical and expected peak loads.
- Provision GPU and CPU pools to meet latency SLOs with acceptable MTTI (mean time to intervention) and pre-warmed capacity.

Process

1) Monthly demand review: each service owner supplies 90/180-day forecast (traffic, model size mix, sequence length distribution).
2) Demand-to-capacity translation: SRE calculates required GPU-hours, batch sizing impact, and KV cache sizing.
3) Buffer policy: maintain 20% headroom on hosted pools for burst, plus a 2-hour reserved burst for predictable events. For Dedicated customers, follow contract SLAs and reserved capacity agreements.
4) Quarterly capacity runbook: run the capacity simulation (see example commands below) and generate scaling recommendations.

Example commands & checks

- Query recent p95 latency and traffic: 
  - grafana or prometheus query examples: 
    - promql: rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",status=~"2.."}[5m])
    - promql: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-api"}[5m])) by (le))
- Run capacity simulator: ./tools/capacity-sim --model gpt-13b --qps 1200 --seq-dist seq-dist.yml --output report.html

Reliability initiatives and backlog prioritization

- All velocity-impacting reliability items should be classified and triaged in the SRE backlog. Typical initiative types: caching improvements, batching efficiency, kernel optimization, model quantization evaluation, regional failover.
- Initiative prioritization matrix: expected SLO improvement vs. engineering effort and customer impact.

Incident review standards

Post-incident process (for Sev2+ and notable burns)

1) Incident write-up: incident lead prepares an incident summary within 48 hours: timeline, impact, mitigation, root cause hypothesis.
2) RCA workshop: within 72 hours involve stakeholders, generate final RCA with evidence, and assign action items.
3) Action item SLAs: owners must acknowledge within 48 hours and complete high-priority items within 14 days or provide a remediation plan.
4) Publish: final postmortem must be published to Confluence with a severity classification, tags, related runbooks, and checklist of completed actions.

Required postmortem sections

- Title, severity, detection time, mitigation time, impact summary (customers affected, duration), timeline (minute-granular), root cause analysis, contributing factors, corrective actions, follow-ups, and metrics showing recovery.

Runbook standards and template

Runbook properties

- Short name (dash-separated), owner, on-call contact, last-reviewed date, and minimal steps to detect, mitigate, and escalate.
- Shell commands and dashboard links must be included.
- Keep runbooks under 1 page of steps; link to deeper diagnostics when necessary.

Canonical runbook template (fields)

1) Runbook title
2) Service & component
3) Owner & escalation path
4) Symptoms / how detected (metrics/alerts)
5) Immediate mitigation steps (ordered, numbered)
6) Diagnostic commands and queries
7) Post-incident actions and links to postmortem template

Sample runbook: "inference-api-high-p99"

- Symptoms: p99 > 2.5s for 5m OR p95 > 1.2s for 15m.
- Immediate actions (numbered):
  1. Confirm alert on Grafana SLO panel and check burn-rate dashboard.
  2. Check NGINX / envoy 5xx rate: promql: increase(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{status!~"2.."}[5m])
  3. Check GPU pool utilization: promql: avg(gpu_utilization{pool=~"prod-"}) by (instance)
  4. If GPU pool saturated and autoscale failed, fail traffic to fallback model variant: curl -X POST $CONTROL_PLANE/route-fallback -d '{"service":"inference-api","variant":"cpu-fallback"}'
  5. If latency due to model cold starts, temporarily increase batch window (coordination with runtime leads) and scale up pre-warmed instances.
  6. Open incident, notify product, and tag the postmortem owner.

- Diagnostic queries and data to collect: trace IDs for slow requests, representative request payloads, model versions involved, region, and client ids.

Review and continuous improvement

- Annual audit of all SLOs to ensure alignment with business goals.
- Quarterly runbook drills for top 10 critical services (tabletop or fire-drill).
- Monthly reliability report summarizing SLO attainment, notable burns, and progress on reliability backlog.

Appendix: links and artifacts

- SLO dashboard template: https://grafana.redwood/slo-template
- Burn-rate alert playbook: https://confluence.redwood/eng-sre/burn-rate-playbook
- Runbook JSON storage: https://confluence.redwood/eng-sre/runbooks
- Capacity simulator repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/capacity-sim.git

If you are a service owner and have questions about applying these standards, please contact the SRE lead (sre-lead@redwood.ai) or file an RFC in the eng-sre space.
